assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) gave a tractable account of how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. The financial-accelerator work of Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist is the other half of the credit-friction paradigm. This framework underlies modern macro-finance, crisis models and policy analysis, and shows up widely in central-bank and financial-stability work. It rests on a clear theoretical insight with broad applications.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler is the strongest credited name on the accelerator and its monetary-policy and banking extensions. Gilchrist is more an empirical and applied contributor. Bernanke is not on this list and was recognised in 2022 for banks and financial crises, so the credit lines need careful drawing to avoid overlap.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are about 30 years old. The framework has been tested and extended heavily, including in the 2008 crisis and its aftermath, and has become standard. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and crises, and whether the committee sees this as distinct enough.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist, rather than only Kiyotaki and Moore, should be credited.
Direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz (2003) transformed trade theory and empirics by putting firm heterogeneity and selection at the centre, showing gains from trade via reallocation across firms. Helpman's firm-level and monopolistic-competition trade models, including with Melitz and Yeaple, extend the framework. It reoriented a whole field and is tightly tied to firm-level data. The framework is used heavily in policy work on trade liberalisation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the key originator of the heterogeneous-firm model. Helpman has the broader foundational record across new trade theory, firm heterogeneity and, with Grossman, political economy and growth. Redding has made important contributions to quantitative and spatial trade but is a later extension and omitted from the proposal for sharper credit.
assessment.maturity: More than 20 years of confirmation, large empirical validation and many extensions. Krugman's 2008 prize covered earlier new trade theory, so this is a distinct, mature advance.
uncertainties: Whether Melitz's relative youth and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Eaton-Kortum strands complicate the credit.
Whether the committee prefers to pair Helpman with Grossman (B031) instead.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance programme established empirically that legal protection of investors shapes financial development, ownership structure and corporate governance, and it opened a large cross-country research agenda in finance, law and institutions. The papers are among the most cited in economics. The findings have been influential in policy and development debates.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are the La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny collaborations. Shleifer is the common thread, with broader contributions in behavioural finance and limits to arbitrage. A three-person limit forces leaving out Vishny, who is a genuine co-author on the foundational papers, so the credit is imperfect.
assessment.maturity: The work is 25+ years old and has been thoroughly scrutinised and refined.
uncertainties: Substantial methodological criticism of the legal-origins identification, including coding of shareholder-rights indices and causality.
Whether the committee considers the empirical contribution durable enough given critiques.
Excluding Vishny and the broader Shleifer record complicates the right laureate set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock work and the task-based approach to technology showed how trade and technology reshape local labour markets, polarisation and wage inequality. The results changed academic and political debate on globalisation and automation, and relied on well-identified, transparent empirical designs with high policy salience.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task-based and trade-shock strands. Autor-Dorn-Hanson is the core team for the China shock. Katz's contributions on skill-biased technical change and supply and demand for skill are significant but partially overlap with the 2023 prize for Goldin, and the task framework also has Acemoglu-Restrepo antecedents outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock papers date from roughly 2013 and have many replications and extensions. Some of the longer-run conclusions are still being contested.
uncertainties: Is the China-shock evidence mature enough, given continuing debate about long-run adjustment?
Credit across the task framework (Acemoglu, Autor, Levy, Murnane) is not fully captured by this list.
Katz's role is omitted for a three-name limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, together with the Taylor rule, is the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis and underpins inflation-targeting practice. Woodford provided the most complete theoretical synthesis. Gali, Gertler and Clarida contributed the canonical NK Phillips curve and policy analysis. Practical influence on central banks is large.
assessment.attribution: The credit is highly diffuse across at least eight listed names plus others, including Calvo, Rotemberg, Fischer and Taylor in earlier contributions, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans (CEE) on estimation, and Smets-Wouters. Choosing three is hard, and any selection leaves out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use. Some of the framework's relevance was tested by the post-2021 inflation episode, with mixed evidence.
uncertainties: A severe attribution problem across a diffuse literature.
Whether the committee sees this as covered by earlier macro prizes.
Post-pandemic inflation has raised questions about aspects of the framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Manski's work on partial identification and the reflection problem reframed what can be inferred under weak assumptions and the role of credibility in empirical research. Tamer and Molinari extended it into a practical inference toolkit used in structural work, notably with incomplete models and moment inequalities. It is conceptually deep, though its adoption is narrower than that of mainstream methods.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator. Tamer (2003) and Molinari are principal contributors to the inference theory, but the field also includes Chernozhukov, Hong, Tamer and Imbens-Manski, among others, so credit beyond Manski is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundations date from the late 1980s and 1990s, and the field has matured since. Econometrics was recognised recently by the 2021 prize (Imbens), so competition within the subfield is notable.
uncertainties: Whether the committee values methodology that is less visible in applied research.
How to credit Tamer versus Molinari versus others.
Age and timing for Manski.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers model (1982) is the foundation of non-cooperative bargaining theory. Rubinstein-Wolinsky and Binmore-Rubinstein-Wolinsky link bargaining to decentralised markets, and the model has been used extensively in labour, search and political economy. It has a clean, durable theoretical insight.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator. Wolinsky is a strong co-contributor on markets, and Binmore has contributed to extensions and the Nash programme. Shaked-Sutton is a related contribution not on this list.
assessment.maturity: More than 40 years old and fully absorbed into the canon. Game theory has been recognised many times, including in 2020 for auctions, so field balance is a consideration.
uncertainties: Possible field fatigue after repeated game-theory prizes.
The impact is concentrated in theory, with fewer direct empirical or policy applications.
Whether Binmore, rather than Wolinsky, should be the second credited name.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Duffie's work on credit-risk modelling, affine asset pricing and OTC market structure, including Duffie-Garleanu-Pedersen (2005) search-based OTC markets, provides core tools for understanding market liquidity, intermediation and market design. It also had practical influence on post-crisis regulation and derivatives market reform. It is serious and useful, but the contribution is more a body of work than a single transformative idea.
assessment.attribution: Duffie is the central figure across credit risk and OTC markets. Garleanu and Pedersen are the key co-authors of the search-in-OTC framework. Pedersen's wider contributions on liquidity are covered in B050, so there is overlap. Credit for credit-risk modelling also includes Singleton, Lando and Jarrow, who are outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are 20+ years old, with extensive follow-on work and regulatory uptake. Maturity is adequate, though a single anchoring discovery is less clear than for the higher-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: No single unifying breakthrough compared with higher-ranked candidates.
Attribution beyond Duffie is uncertain given the broad finance literature.
Finance has been recognised repeatedly (2013, 2022), and relative merit across candidates is hard to compare. I disclose a finance-specialist perspective.
